name: Zilpaterol (Zilmax)

lead: Zilpaterol is a beta-2 adrenergic agonist fed to feedlot cattle in the last weeks before slaughter to increase muscle yield and feed efficiency. It is sold as Zilmax.
It is sometimes mentioned alongside clenbuterol as a related beta-agonist, but the sources reviewed describe only veterinary use and contain no human trials or community accounts.

paras: As a beta-2 agonist it shifts nutrient use in cattle toward lean muscle rather than fat. Cattle studies report greater carcass weight, leaner carcasses and better feed efficiency.

No human safety data for deliberate use exist in the sources. In cattle, a 2013 episode in which animals arrived at a Tyson plant with missing hooves in hot weather led to Tyson refusing Zilmax-fed cattle. Some studies report lower meat tenderness. It is prescription-only in Canada and Australia and banned for livestock in several countries.

lead: Zilpaterol is a synthetic beta-2 adrenergic agonist given orally to cattle under the brand name Zilmax, produced by Merck's animal-health unit Intervet. It is fed during the last three to six weeks in a feedlot, with a withdrawal period before slaughter, to increase muscle mass and feed efficiency. [1][2]

No human clinical studies of zilpaterol were identified; published research concerns cattle performance, carcass traits and meat quality. [3][4][5][6] Its mention in appearance-related contexts is as a veterinary relative of clenbuterol, but the literature reviewed contains no documentation of human use.
infobox: Approved for cattle in about 17 countries; banned in China, Russia, Taiwan, many EU states

paras: Zilpaterol is a veterinary feed additive. Feedlot trials have tested it in steers and heifers to increase growth performance and carcass yield. [5][7]

A meta-analysis of zilpaterol and ractopamine effects in cattle examined feedlot performance, carcass traits and shear force of meat. [6] Trials report improved carcass characteristics in cattle fed zilpaterol, with some reporting increases in shear force (reduced tenderness) compared with controls. [3][4][6]
Wikipedia notes that some studies found no meaningful flavor or juiciness differences while others found reduced tenderness and marbling. [1]
As of 2017 zilpaterol was approved in 17 countries including the US, Canada, South Africa, South Korea, Ukraine and Brazil, while China, Taiwan, Russia and many EU countries ban it. [1]
In August 2013 Tyson Foods announced it would no longer accept Zilmax-fed cattle after animals arrived at its plants with missing hooves during hot weather. [1]

No studies found in humans. Controlled research is limited to cattle trials, which compare zilpaterol with control diets and with ractopamine and clenbuterol on growth and carcass measures. [3][4][5][6]

timeline.event: Major US meatpackers adopt Zilmax-fed cattle. [1]
Tyson Foods stops accepting Zilmax-fed cattle after the missing-hooves reports. [1]
